title: "Scaling Law"
description: "An empirical relationship describing how model performance changes with scale such as data, parameters, or compute."
term: "Scaling Law"
letter: "S"
category: "LLM Engineering"
difficulty: "Advanced"
---

## Simple explanation

A scaling law describes a pattern in how a model's performance changes as
resources such as training data, model size, or compute increase. It can
help estimate the likely benefit of scaling, but it does not promise that
every larger model will be better.

## Technical explanation

Scaling laws are empirical fits relating a metric—often held-out loss—to
quantities such as parameter count, dataset size, and compute. Some
relationships follow approximate power laws over a measured regime. The
fit may not extrapolate when data quality, architecture, training recipe,
or evaluation distribution changes.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Scaling estimates inform compute allocation and model-training plans.
They can help compare investments, but must be balanced with data quality,
serving cost, latency, and task-specific performance.

## How it works

Researchers train models or run experiments at multiple scales, measure a
consistent outcome, and fit a functional relationship. Predictions should
include uncertainty and be validated near the intended scale rather than
assuming the fitted trend holds indefinitely.

## Practical example

A team can use results from smaller training runs to estimate whether a
larger run is likely to reduce validation loss enough to justify its
compute cost. It should also evaluate downstream tasks, since language
model loss is not identical to product utility.

## Common misconceptions

- Scaling laws are empirical trends, not physical laws that guarantee
  performance improvements for all settings.
- More parameters alone do not ensure better outcomes; data, compute,
  training, and evaluation matter.
